# Selection — TRD §15 row 7: checkpoint construction, cadence and retention

**Status:** selected, and folded into the TRD. **Date:** 2026-08-19
**Closes:** TRD §15 row 7 · **Scope of:** review 3b (protocol)
**Constrained by:** TRD §7.6, §7.5, §13.2, §13.7, §10.1, §12, §11.3 · **Stage:** [sequencing.md](../sequencing.md) §3.5
**Vectors:** [`test/vectors/checkpoint.json`](../../test/vectors/checkpoint.json), generated by
[`scripts/generate-checkpoint-vectors.mjs`](../../scripts/generate-checkpoint-vectors.mjs)
**Companions:** [row 8](./row-8-attribution-record.md) had to be selected first, and discharges this row's
hardest constraint; [row 5](./row-5-finalization.md) supplies the head vector the manifest carries;
[row 9](./row-9-chain-head-discovery.md) supplies the epoch-head pairing.
**Amended by:** [`S0-2`](../review/remediation/S0-2/README.md) (2026-08-27) — the retention interlock gains a fourth clause. Its subject was corrected from the checkpoint to
the generation, and TRD §13.7 now states the predicate that enforces it: no generation is dropped while a retained
checkpoint sealed under it lacks a surviving authorized opener. That is what keeps §11.3 test 8's fallback openable.
**Amended by:** [`S0-5`](../review/remediation/S0-5/README.md) (2026-08-27) — the manifest's `{sv, ds}` is **re-derived locally by every restorer** rather than believed, and
the accepted-head baseline gains a `SemanticAdmission` signed before any pre-checkpoint envelope may be
trimmed. A producer may admit its own proposal where no second eligible client exists, and the record says
so (TRD §7.6).
**Amended by:** [`S0-6`](../review/remediation/S0-6/README.md) (2026-08-27) — a checkpoint travelling in a package is admitted through the same path as one restored
locally: coverage re-derived by the importer, then the admission verified (TRD §7.6).
**Amended by:** the [`S0-5` return](../review/remediation/S0-5/README.md) (2026-08-28, `FU-11` and the
`k-checkpoint` census entry) — the admission's verifier resolves from the certified set at the manifest's
epoch, never from a presented key; a producer self-admission is refused while that set holds a second
eligible client, and `self_admitted` equals the derived relation in both directions. `K_cp` gains a fresh
16-byte per-seal salt — one message per derived key, §13.8's discipline at the fifth subkey — because a
checkpoint's key must open on every device and so can narrow to a seal but never to a store. And install is a
staged machine: content commits durably first, one activation flips content and heads together, and the
second-newest fallback installs through the same machine (TRD §7.6).

---

## The selection


**2026-09-11 encoding amendment.** Manifest and SemanticAdmission are v2; checkpoint cipher/AAD
remains v1. The two descriptor fields bind separate SHA-256 hashes of decoded opaque bytes,
while full raw descriptors remain required and are rederived by every restorer. The private
adapter bounds each SV/DS pair to 16 MiB combined before hashing or admission progress.
Private v1 completions/receipts and mixed versions refuse without rewriting retained state;
pre-completion requests/offers may resume. See [the compatibility and bounds contract](../account-admission-bounds.md).

```
The checkpoint          one full snapshot, sealed under one generation

  ct = AES-256-GCM( K_cp ; a Yjs full snapshot of the content root, AAD )

  K_cp = HKDF-SHA256(ikm = K_g, salt = cp_salt[16],
                     info = LP("done/checkpoint/v1") || LP(workspace_id), L = 32)

  cp_salt = 16 fresh random bytes PER SEAL, carried in the clear beside the
            nonce. One message per derived key is the key's entire invocation
            discipline (§13.8's, at the fifth subkey): a checkpoint must open
            on every device, so K_cp can narrow to a seal but never to a
            store, and freshness rides the seal instead of a counter no
            single store could keep. The k-checkpoint census entry holds it.

  AAD  = LP("done/cp/v1") || LP(dec v) || LP(workspace_id) || LP(dec gen)
         || LP(dec epoch)

  The snapshot includes row 8's attribution records, because they are content.

The manifest            signed by the producing credential

  M = LP("done/cp-manifest/v2") || LP("2") || LP(workspace_id)
      || LP(dec epoch) || LP(hex epoch_head) || LP(dec gen)
      || LP(hex checkpoint_digest) || LP(hex SHA-256(sv)) || LP(hex SHA-256(ds))
      || LP(hex head_vector_digest) || LP(producing_credential)

  checkpoint_digest = SHA-256(ct)   — the durable store checks it with no key
  sv, ds            — opaque bytes; BOTH bound, and separately. PUBLISHED here,
                      DERIVED by whoever reads: a restorer materialises the
                      snapshot, recomputes them, and refuses a mismatch. That
                      check needs no signature and is not optional.

The admission           what the producer's signature does NOT say

  A = LP("done/cp-admit/v2") || LP("2") || LP(workspace_id)
      || LP(hex checkpoint_digest) || LP(hex manifest_digest)
      || LP(hex SHA-256(derived_sv)) || LP(hex SHA-256(derived_ds))
      || LP(hex head_baseline_digest) || LP(derivation_version)
      || LP(admitting_credential) || LP(dec self_admitted)
      || LP(hex decision_parent)

  sig = Ed25519( the admitting client's signing credential ; A )

  Signed BEFORE any pre-checkpoint envelope may be trimmed.

  derived_sv/ds     what the admitter got by materialising the snapshot, not
                    copied from the manifest. Restorer, admitter and manifest
                    must all three agree.
  head_baseline     the one trusted field. Proving the head vector does not
                    reach past the snapshot needs the accepted events, which
                    trim removes -- so confidence in it IS confidence in the
                    admitting credential, and nothing here pretends otherwise.
  derivation_version  sv and ds are a library's encoding. Unversioned, a change
                      to it turns every stored admission into a silent mismatch.
  self_admitted     single-owner authority (row 11, §13.5) means the only
                    eligible client may be the producer. A second one admits
                    where it exists; otherwise this says so. Requiring two would
                    leave a one-device workspace unable to checkpoint at all.
  eligibility       the verifier resolves from the certified set at the
                    manifest's epoch (S0-2's member entries) -- a lookup,
                    refusing an uncertified credential before any signature
                    runs. self_admitted equals the derived producer relation
                    in both directions, and a producer self-admission is
                    REFUSED while the set holds a second eligible client
                    (the S0-5 return; the set and producer are published
                    vector inputs).
  decision_parent   incomparable proposals serialise here. NEVER by wall clock.
  head_vector       = empty at first genesis; otherwise for each credential ASCENDING BY ID:
                        LP(credential_id) || LP(dec seq) || LP(hex link)
                      digest = SHA-256( LP("done/headvec/v1") || head_vector )

Cadence

  Forced      A rotation produces a checkpoint under the new generation
              BEFORE the old generation may be dropped.
  Tunable     Otherwise, the first of an accepted-position count or an
              elapsed interval. Both are grounded in first-sync cost and
              neither can be set honestly before there is a service.

Retention

  At least two checkpoints and their suffixes (§11.3 test 8).
  Never drop a generation while any retained checkpoint is sealed under it
  and has no surviving authorized opener. Stated over OPENERS rather than
  the local KeyEnvelope: a retained recovery or reader wrap may still open a
  generation whose envelope is gone (TRD §13.7).

Install                 staged, and activation is one commit (the S0-5 return)

  Content commits durably into its slot first, under a durable install
  record, visible to nothing; one activation then flips the live pair --
  content root and accepted-head baseline -- together or not at all. A kill
  before the activation activates NEITHER; recovery completes from the
  record or rolls the stage back, never serving a mixture. Trim reads the
  ACTIVE pair, so only an admitted, activated tuple licenses it. A newest
  tuple missing bytes, admission or opener is refused and the second-newest
  complete tuple is installed through the same machine.

                LP(s) = uint16be(byteLength(utf8 s)) || utf8 s
```

Everything below is why, and what it cost.

---

## 1. §7.6 sets three constraints, and they are satisfied three different ways

That is the useful frame for reading this row, because only one of the three is actually solved here.

| §7.6's _must not happen_                                    | How it is satisfied                                                                                                           |
| ----------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| No merged state as the recovery representation              | **Here.** One full snapshot under one generation, plus a manifest that makes it usable by a store that understands none of it |
| No bare state vector as a coverage claim                    | **Here.** `sv` and `ds` bound separately, with a negative each                                                                |
| No checkpoint that re-signs another credential's operations | **By [row 8](./row-8-attribution-record.md)**, and this is why that row had to come first                                     |

**The third is the one worth dwelling on.** §7.6 calls the flattening shape _"exactly what §7.4's no-re-signing
rule prohibits, arriving through a performance optimization"_ — a rule that must be remembered, by whoever writes
the checkpoint, every time. With row 8, attribution is a set of standing records each signed by its own author,
sitting in the content the snapshot covers. **The producing credential signs the container and nothing inside
it.** The forbidden shape stops being prohibited and becomes unreachable: there is no step at which anyone could
re-sign anything, because nothing needs re-signing.

That is the whole argument for the ordering in §15's _close next_ note, and it held.

---

## 2. Both coverage halves, bound separately, and why that needs two negatives

§7.6 is unusually specific here:

> A Yjs state vector maps client to clock over **insertions**; deletions live separately in the `DeleteSet`. Two
> replicas can carry identical state vectors and disagree about what has been deleted, so "the checkpoint's state
> vector is dominated" does not mean "everything the checkpoint contains is here".

So the manifest binds `{sv, ds}`. **The vectors publish that as a pair of negatives rather than one**, and the
coverage audit is what forced it: the first pass had a negative changing `ds` alone and none changing `sv` alone,
so `sv` was bound and tested by nothing. Both now exist, and the pair is the point — either one alone is exactly
the claim §7.6 says is not a coverage claim.

**Both are bound as opaque byte strings, and that is deliberate.** Their content is Yjs's, and §10.1 carries a
deferred v13 → v14 upgrade that would change it. Binding them opaquely means that upgrade changes what the bytes
say rather than what this construction is — which matters because §10.1 also says the upgrade must not land
during Stage 4, and a manifest format that had to change with it would make that constraint worse.

---

## 3. The head vector, and the sort that is load-bearing

The manifest carries [row 5](./row-5-finalization.md)'s accepted-head vector: for every credential, where its
chain had got to, with row 5 §9's first-genesis-only empty-vector exception. Certification still names the
creating member; an explicit member-at-zero entry is not an alternate serialization. That is what lets
a device starting from a checkpoint verify the suffix forward from
authenticated heads instead of replaying every chain from genesis — the composition §7.5 predicted when it said
the log shape _"composes with §7.6's manifest"_.

**The serialization is sorted ascending by credential id, and the sort is not tidiness.** Two devices producing
a checkpoint over the same accepted state must produce the same digest; a map iterated in insertion order would
not, and the disagreement would look like a corrupted manifest rather than a canonicalization bug. There is a
negative for it.

**`epoch` and `epoch_head` are both bound**, on [row 9](./row-9-chain-head-discovery.md)'s reasoning: the head
commits to the number, so binding both costs two bytes and means a current-looking number can never be paired
with an older head. It matters more here than anywhere, because for a device restoring from a checkpoint **this
manifest is the first authenticated thing it reads.**

---

## 4. Cadence: one forced rule and two honest tunables

**The forced rule falls out of key retention and is easy to miss.** A checkpoint is sealed under one generation
and is openable only while that generation is retained. Row 8 removed the _attribution_ reason to retain old
generations, and §6.1's trim removes the store's. So a rotation that dropped the old generation while the newest
checkpoint was still sealed under it would **destroy the recovery path in the course of tidying up**. Therefore:

> **A rotation produces a checkpoint under the new generation before the old generation may be dropped.**

That is not a cadence preference; it is an ordering constraint between two operations that otherwise look
independent, and it is the kind of thing found at a restore rather than at a review.

**The other two triggers are tunables and are stated as such.** An accepted-position count and an elapsed
interval, whichever comes first. Their ground is first-sync cost: §12 budgets checkpoint verification at 1.5 s,
and what the cadence actually controls is **how long a suffix a fresh device must replay after it.** Naming a
number now would give it an authority no measurement supports, and there is no service to measure against — the
same treatment PRD §11 q6 gives the card-split threshold, for the same reason.

---

## 5. Retention: two, and a rule about generations

**At least two checkpoints and their suffixes**, because §11.3 test 8 is explicit: _"Repeat with the store
holding the newest checkpoint unavailable, falling back to the next-newest retained checkpoint and its suffix."_
A retention policy of one makes that test unpassable by construction, which is the sort of thing worth checking
a policy against before writing it rather than after.

**And: never drop a generation while any retained checkpoint is sealed under it.** This is the mirror of §4's
forced rule and closes the same hole from the other side. Together they are the whole interlock between
checkpoint retention and key retention, which §13.7 warns must not be conflated with local-store retention — and
now needs one sentence in each direction rather than a general caution.

**The subject of that sentence is the generation, and it has to be.** An earlier wording made it the checkpoint —
*never drop a checkpoint whose generation any retained checkpoint still needs* — which reads as an interlock and
is not one: the only checkpoint that needs `g` is the one sealed under `g`, so the rule constrained a checkpoint
by reference to itself and said nothing at all about the key. §4's forced rule guarantees that a checkpoint exists
under the new generation before the old one is dropped; it does not keep the **second-newest** checkpoint
openable, and that is exactly the one §11.3 test 8 falls back to. Dropping `g` while `C_g` is still the mandated
fallback leaves an authentic, intact, undecryptable checkpoint and fails that test by construction.

**What still needs selecting is what counts as an opener.** A local `KeyEnvelope` is not the only path to `K_g` —
a retained recovery wrap or reader wrap may keep a generation openable after the local envelope is gone — so
"dropping a generation" has to name the set of objects whose removal actually ends access, and §13.7's deletion
predicate has to read that set rather than a single carrier. That inventory belongs with the generation-reference
accounting that rotate, revoke and replace-recovery all need (§15 row 15), and it is not settled here.

---

## 6. What it costs

| Cost                   | Size                                                                        |
| ---------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Per checkpoint, client | One snapshot, one AES-GCM seal, one SHA-256, one Ed25519 signature          |
| Per checkpoint, store  | **One hash.** No content key, no parsing (§7.2's boundary, again)           |
| Manifest size          | Two identifiers, four small integers, three digests and the coverage pair   |
| Retained               | Two checkpoints and two suffixes rather than one                            |
| Bundle                 | **Nothing.** All four primitives are WebCrypto (row 1)                      |
| A fifth §13.2 subkey   | One label plus 16 salt bytes per seal. `done/checkpoint/v1`, differing from the other four by name — and by deriving per seal, which is what buys its invocation discipline without a counter |

**The store's cost is the line worth reading**, for the same reason it was in [row 4](./row-4-envelope-format.md):
a content-blind durable store that had to do more than hash would be negotiating the content-blindness boundary
rather than drawing it, which is [sequencing.md](../sequencing.md) §7's named warning sign for Stage 4.

---

## 7. What Stage 4 owes, and what is not in this row

**Who produces a checkpoint, and what happens when two devices produce one concurrently.** Two valid manifests
at the same epoch over different snapshots are not a conflict — each is a true statement about what its producer
had seen — but the store needs a rule for which it serves and the client needs a rule for which it uses.
**Newest-by-head-vector rather than newest-by-clock** is the shape that follows from everything above, since a
clock is not evidence (row 9) and the head vector is. Stating it properly needs the durable store's interface,
which is Stage 4's.

**One obligation with a security purpose.** A checkpoint that fails any check must be **refused and reported, and
the next-newest used** — never partially applied. §11.3 test 8 is the test; the rule matters because a
half-applied checkpoint is a state no replica ever held, and it would converge with the others as though it were
real. **Since the `S0-5` return this is a machine rather than an obligation**: the staged install's activation
is the only step that makes anything live, `test/storageSchedule.test.ts` schedules a kill and a second writer
inside its window, and the fallback assertion is an install receipt — the older complete tuple's content and
heads land through the same two commits — not opener arithmetic.

**Not in this row.** The records inside the snapshot are [row 8](./row-8-attribution-record.md)'s. The links and
heads the vector collects are [row 5](./row-5-finalization.md)'s. What a migration or terminal package carries —
including the signed head row 9 requires — is **row 10**'s. How deep the suffix is retained beside each
checkpoint is **row 6**'s, and this row hands it the same interlock: never shorter than the oldest retained
checkpoint's head vector.

---

## 8. The vectors

`node scripts/generate-checkpoint-vectors.mjs` writes them; `--check` fails if they are stale, and `pnpm check`
now runs it with the other ten.

**One checkpoint and nineteen manifest-and-seal negatives, plus twenty-two at the admission.** A laptop
checkpointing a two-device workspace at epoch 9, generation 3 — the sealed snapshot, its digest, the sorted
head vector and its digest, the signed manifest, and (since `S0-5`) the admission with its published
eligibility inputs.

**Sixteen of the manifest-and-seal negatives are the two bound field lists**, one per field: five in the
sealed checkpoint's AAD and eleven in the manifest. The other three are the checks that are not field
bindings: a manifest whose digest does not match the bytes beside it, which the store catches with no key, a
wrong workspace subkey, and — since the `S0-5` return — a wrong per-seal salt, which is the `k-checkpoint`
discipline refusing as a value. The admission's four authority negatives (uncertified credential,
self-admission beside a second eligible, and the honest flag in both directions) carry genuine signatures on
purpose: each asserts its own signature verifies before relying on the refusal, so the refusal provably comes
from the lookup, the cardinality rule, or the flag rule — never from broken bytes.

**Three of them are §7.6's own sentences as values.** `coverage-ignores-deletions` and
`coverage-ignores-insertions` are the pair that makes _a bare state vector is not a coverage claim_ checkable in
both directions. `produced-by-another-credential` covers both halves of that name — a forged signature, and the
producer's name changed inside a genuine one.

**The coverage audit refused the first pass twice, and both were real.** `checkpoint_digest` had only the
store's keyless hash check testing it, which is a different check in a different place and survives a store that
does not run it; and `sv` had no isolating negative at all while `ds` did, which is precisely the asymmetry §7.6
warns about, reproduced by accident in the file meant to test for it.
